extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate public interested in literature, education, and manners (aspiring poets, critics, parents/educators)
extracted.subtask_description: A periodical essay-style literary criticism focused mainly on evaluating Milton's Paradise Lost and on broader rules for epic poetry (probability vs. the marvellous, use of supernatural machinery, style for divine speakers). Also includes contemporaneous commentary on education and manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a subject conformable to the poet's genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace advises a Poet to consider thoroughly the Nature and Force of his Genius; Milton seems to have known perfectly well, wherein his Strength lay, and has therefore chosen a Subject entirely conformable to those Talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a subject that fits the poet's dominant talents — do not force a subject unsuited to your imaginative strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject grandeur to the poet's capacity for the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: As his Genius was wonderfully turned to the Sublime, his Subject is the noblest that could have entered into the Thoughts of Man. Every thing that is truly great and astonishing has a place in it (the whole System of the intellectual World; the Chaos, and the Creation; Heaven, Earth and Hell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For poets inclined to the sublime, choose the largest, most elevated subjects available and populate them with vast and astonishing elements appropriate to that aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict divine persons with restraint and orthodoxy
rubrics_metrics.description: If Milton's Majesty forsakes him any where, it is in those Parts of his Poem, where the Divine Persons are introduced as Speakers. The Author proceeds with a kind of Fear and Trembling, whilst he describes the Sentiments of the Almighty; he dares not give his Imagination its full Play, but chooses to confine himself to such Thoughts as are drawn from the Books of the most Orthodox Divines, and to such Expressions as may be met with in Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When putting words into divine or sacred mouths, prefer devout, scriptural, and theologically orthodox diction that evokes devotion and reverence rather than merely poetical grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat abstruse theological points with shortness and perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Particular Beauty of the Speeches in the Third Book consists in that Shortness and Perspicuity of Style, in which the Poet has couched the greatest Mysteries of Christianity (predestination, free-will, grace, incarnation, redemption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle complex doctrinal material concisely and clearly, interspersing poetic graces where the subject admits, so that abstruse matter remains comprehensible and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic fable must combine the probable and the marvellous
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle observes that the Fable of an Epic Poem should abound in Circumstances that are both credible and astonishing; the Fable should be filled with the Probable and the Marvellous. If the Fable is only Probable, it differs nothing from a true History; if it is only Marvellous, it is no better than a Romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance: provide enough plausibility to secure the reader's belief while including wondrous incidents that inspire admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use supernatural machinery to render miracles credible
rubrics_metrics.description: The next Method of reconciling Miracles with Credibility is by a happy Invention of the Poet; in particular, when he introduces Agents of a superior Nature (the gods), who are capable of effecting what is wonderful and not to be met with in the ordinary course of things (examples: Homer, Virgil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you include miraculous or extraordinary events, attribute them to intelligible supernatural agents or a coherent system of causes so the marvels feel plausible within the poem's world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid marvellous events without a credible cause
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be any Instance in the Æneid liable to Exception it is where Æneas is represented as tearing up the Myrtle that dropped Blood; this seems to have the Marvellous without the Probable because it is represented as proceeding from Natural Causes, without the Interposition of any God or supernatural power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present astonishing events as if they arose from mere natural causes when such origins strain plausibility; supply a credible (often supernatural) explanation or avoid the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the plain literal sense appears probable to ordinary readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the hidden Meaning of an Epic Allegory, the plain literal Sense ought to appear Probable. The Story should be such as an ordinary Reader may acquiesce in, whatever Natural, Moral, or Political Truth may be discovered in it by Men of greater Penetration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even allegorical or supernatural narratives must retain a surface plausibility so that general readers can accept the story without suspension of disbelief that breaks the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dreamlike, shadowy episodes that lack credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Limbo of Vanity, the Episode of Sin and Death, and some of the imaginary Persons in Chaos are astonishing but not credible; they are descriptions of dreams and shadows, not of things or persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of passages that read as mere reverie or unintelligible allegory; ensure imaginary elements have intelligible form and function within the fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor fiction in recognizable or historical elements to increase credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: This Appearance of Probability is so absolutely requisite in the greater kinds of Poetry, that Aristotle observes the Ancient Tragick Writers made use of the Names of such great Men as had actually lived in the World, tho the Tragedy proceeded upon Adventures they were never engaged in, on purpose to make the Subject more Credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use familiar names, conventions, or historical touchstones to give the reader a foothold of belief even when events are fictionalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ vivid, well-chosen imagery and simile to produce grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Satan's Sitting upon the Brink and taking a Survey of the whole Face of Nature, with the Simile illustrating this Circumstance, fills the Mind of the Reader with as surprising and glorious an Idea as any that arises in the whole Poem. His Flight... with the particular Description of the Sun are set forth in all the Wantonness of a luxuriant Imagination. His Shape, Speech and Behaviour upon his transforming himself into an Angel of Light, are touched with exquisite Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rich, fitting imagery and similes to evoke awe and grandeur; ensure the images suit the subject and enhance credibility rather than distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary digressions even if they are beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: The celebrated Complaint with which the Third Book opens and the beautiful Digression upon Hypocrisie may be looked upon as an Excrescence rather than an essential Part of the Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune digressions that do not serve the main fable; beauty alone does not justify a passage if it impedes the poem's coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boarding-school curriculum for young gentlewomen (advertisement specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Boarding-School for young Gentlewomen... where, beside the common Instructions given to young Gentlewomen, they will be taught the whole Art of Paistrey and Preserving, with whatever may render them accomplished. Those who please to make Tryal of the Vigilance and Ability of the Persons concerned may enquire at the two Golden-Balls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A boarding-school for gentlewomen should offer usual accomplishments (needlework, dancing, French) plus practical domestic arts (pastry, preserving) and be judged by the vigilance and ability of its staff and convenience of location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public (college-like) education advantages: lasting friendships and better cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: An Advantage accompanying a Publick way of Education is, that we very often contract such Friendships at School, as are a Service to us all the following Part of our Lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public schooling is recommended for its social networking and for fostering friendships that can benefit pupils later in life; it also prevents promising genius from being spoiled by inadequate local tutorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of private rural masters: either excessive tasks or neglect of classics
rubrics_metrics.description: The first [rural master] imposed much more upon me than my Parts... and used me barbarously for not performing Impossibilities. The latter was of quite another Temper; a Boy who would run upon his Errands... might have as little Conversation with any of the Classicks as he thought fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tutors who either overburden pupils with inappropriate chores or neglect classical instruction; both extremes spoil promising students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief qualification of a good poet/playwright (ironic prescription)
rubrics_metrics.description: Query: Pray be so kind as to let me know what you esteem to be the chief Qualification of a good Poet, especially of one who writes Plays; Answer: To be a very well-bred Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a wittily ironical criterion: social breeding, manners, and decorum are here offered (tongue-in-cheek) as an essential quality alongside literary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for idleness: structure time and daily intellectual habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Idleness is a Distemper. If I had less Leisure, I should have more; one Face of Indolence overspreads the whole... Seneca assures Lucelius there was not a Day in which he did not either write something, or read and epitomize some good Author; Pliny carried a pocket-book while hunting to fill vacancies of Time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter idleness by constraining time with definite occupations, keep daily habits of writing/reading/epitomizing authors, and use pockets of idle time productively.
